items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I made a conscious effort to play trios. So I did a trio with Art Hodes and Don DeMicheal, and then they died. And then it was Ralph Sutton and Gus Johnson and Gus Johnson died.

ctx.x: That’s something to sustain a band like that too without a bass player I think.

Oh we were brilliant. We really enjoyed. I made a conscious effort to play trios. So I did a trio with Art Hodes and Don DeMicheal, and then they died. And then it was Ralph Sutton and Gus Johnson and Gus Johnson died. Then I did one with Dick Wellstood and Bobby Rosengarden, and Dick died. And then, you know, but after a while, so like I switched to guitars. And they’re all alive. In fact we’re going to do it tonight, the Breezin’ Along group. I’ll have fun with that. Because Howard Alden can read my mind, Bucky…

items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I was really not the leader I was more or less flung into it. When you have Scott and Warren and Ralph and the guys, they’re all natural leaders.

ctx.x: That’s very interesting Mike, thank you. I say thank you because I enjoy being in control. I think that’s number one, you have to enjoy being in control. You have to really believe that the guys that you’re playing with will allow you to be in control and they won’t go kibbitzing around. But I think you have to be an extrovert, which is either you’re introvert or an extrovert, and you can’t do it halfheartedly, otherwise it fails. And the ability to conceive the beginning, the natural beginning of a tune and how…

what it’s probably about. You know, like how much time should you allow or allot a given piece? You know, for the most part though, like last night, well last night was not really a good example of what it was I can do as a leader because I was really not the leader I was more or less flung into it. When you have Scott and Warren and Ralph and the guys, they’re all natural leaders. Each of them wants to be the leader but they’re all being very reticent about taking the bull by the horns and doing it. But I prefer…

That’s what I was going to ask you talk about too because you have a specific stage presence. And I want you to talk about this because you know this music is a combination when you play the blues there’s some sorrow in there, but it can’t be one hundred percent sorrow. And then of course when I see your stage demeanor there’s some humor in there, but it’s not trite, it’s somewhere in the middle. Talk to us about that. Because you have, that’s what I meant that you have a stage presence that, that mixture of…

items.title: Ralph Sutton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995
items.q: You’ve got a great group coming in with Scott Hamilton and Warren Vache, and of course Bob Haggart who we’re going to talk with, and Kenny Davern, and Bobby Rosengarden.

ctx.x: We’re going to have some fun.

You’re going to have some fun. You’ve got a great group coming in with Scott Hamilton and Warren Vache, and of course Bob Haggart who we’re going to talk with, and Kenny Davern, and Bobby Rosengarden. That’s quite a cast. So on behalf of Hamilton College Jazz Archive, I want to thank Ralph Sutton for joining us today. It’s been a real pleasure, and I enjoyed your philosophy on life and music. And thanks for your time.
